Thank you for your quick and thorough reply. It makes sense to me that jump dispersal (in my case, dispersal across long distances) would be a relatively rare event, that the model including this parameter explains the data far better than a model where it is not an option, and that the model incorporating J decreases both D and E. Thanks for the clarifications!

On 09/15/14, Nick Matzke  wrote:
> Forgot to add -- the p-value on the likelihood ratio test is extremely significant for your data (as is common but not universal for biogeography datasets). This means there is a huge likelihood difference. But all this necessarily means is that some/much of your data has much lower probability under the DEC model. Often, DEC has to invoke several events to explain what DEC+J can do in one event. E.g., to get (A(A(A,B)), at some point there has to be a range expansion, A-->AB, and then the correct vicariance event (AB->A,B), or some similar combination, e.g. subset sympatry and then an extinction. 
>
> And, *crucially*, in order to have a range expansion, the d parameter has to be positive. But if d is positive, this lowers the probability of branches starting in A and ending in A, or starting in B and ending in B. As d gets higher, the probability of stasis declines. So if your data indicates a lot of stasis -- clades all living in single areas -- then the likelihood will get worse for those parts of the data as d increases, even if some positive d is required to move lineages around.
>
>
> This effect will get more and more extreme the more data you have, and you have the ranges of several hundred species in your dataset! So, short version: I will definitely never claim that DEC+J is the best possible model, or even a really good model, but it appears that we can say that, often, it's a lot less bad than DEC at explaining the data.
>
>
> Cheers!
